title: People v. Shaw
description: Whether a gun discovered in an apartment should be suppressed because the defendant's arrest violated Payton v New York (a constructive entry) and the tenant's subsequent consent to search was not voluntary or sufficiently attenuated from the illegal arrest.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued there was no Payton violation because the defendant was arrested outside the apartment and lacked standing to challenge the search, and that the tenant's consent was voluntary and attenuated.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued the gun should be suppressed because his arrest violated Payton due to coercive circumstances forcing him out of the apartment, and the tenant's consent to search was not voluntary or sufficiently attenuated from this illegal arrest.
decision_outcome: The court modified the Appellate Division's order, affirming the convictions for murder, attempted murder, and assault, but remitted the case to the Appellate Division to re-evaluate the voluntariness of the tenant's consent to search using the correct legal standard, specifically for the charge of criminal possession of a weapon.

title: Clarke v. Town of Newburgh
description: Whether the Town and Town Board of Newburgh, as a legislatively created political subdivision, can maintain a facial constitutional challenge to the vote dilution provision of the New York Voting Rights Act, with Newburgh arguing they can and the respondents arguing they cannot.
plaintiff_argument: The respondents (original plaintiffs) argued that Newburgh, as a political subdivision, lacks the capacity to sue the State to challenge the constitutionality of the New York Voting Rights Act.
defendant_argument: Newburgh (the appellant) argued that it could bring a facial constitutional challenge to the NYVRA's vote-dilution provision under a 'dilemma' exception, claiming compliance would force it to violate Equal Protection.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, holding that the Town of Newburgh, as a political subdivision, cannot assert a facial constitutional challenge to the New York Voting Rights Act's vote-dilution provision.

title: People v. Sargeant
description: Whether a defendant may forfeit the constitutional right to a trial by a jury of 12 persons by engaging in egregious misconduct, with the plaintiff arguing that such misconduct leads to forfeiture and the defendant arguing against it, seeking a mistrial.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the defendant forfeited his right to a trial by a jury of 12 due to his egregious misconduct of intentionally tampering with a deliberating juror, which necessitated the juror's discharge and left no alternate jurors.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that he did not waive his right to a 12-person jury and that continuing with 11 jurors would be inappropriate, contending that a single instance of misconduct should not result in the forfeiture of this right.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, holding that the trial court properly exercised its discretion in proceeding with the remaining 11 jurors after the defendant forfeited his right to a 12-person jury through egregious misconduct.

title: Onondaga v. New York
description: Whether the Even Year Election Law (EYEL) is an unconstitutional exercise of legislative authority that violates the home rule provisions of Article IX of the State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the EYEL violates Article IX of the State Constitution by infringing on counties' constitutional right to set the timing of county elections and terms of office, and that the EYEL is neither a general nor a duly enacted special law.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the EYEL is constitutional because it is a general law that does not violate Article IX of the State Constitution, and it serves the legitimate state interest of increasing voter turnout and reducing confusion by consolidating local elections with state and federal elections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that the Even Year Election Law is constitutional and does not violate the New York Constitution.

title: Glen Oaks Village Owners v. City of New York
description: Whether New York City's Local Law No. 97, which mandates greenhouse gas emission reductions from large buildings, is preempted by the State's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Local Law No. 97 is preempted by the Climate Act because the State has occupied the field of regulating greenhouse gas emissions.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Local Law No. 97 is not preempted by the Climate Act, as the State legislation does not demonstrate an intent to preclude local regulation.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the Climate Act does not preempt New York City's Local Law No. 97, thereby upholding the City's legislation.

title: Cuomo v. New York State Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government
description: Whether the Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 unconstitutionally vests the State Commission on Ethics and Lobbying in Government with executive power, thereby violating the separation of powers doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the Act is unconstitutional because it empowers the Commission to exercise executive powers without sufficient gubernatorial accountability, specifically regarding the appointment and removal of commissioners.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that New York's constitution permits the Legislature to vest executive power with politically independent bodies to enforce ethics and lobbying laws against executive officials, requiring such autonomy.
decision_outcome: The Court of Appeals reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the Ethics Commission Reform Act of 2022 is not unconstitutional on its face and does not violate the separation of powers doctrine.

title: Amedure v. State
description: Whether Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g), which mandates that a ballot be cast and canvassed if a bipartisan local board is split on its validity, violates the equal representation mandate of the New York Constitution and principles of judicial review.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) violates the equal representation mandate in article II, section 8 of the New York Constitution by allowing a ballot to be processed as valid even if the bipartisan board is split, and improperly restricts judicial review, potentially enabling electoral fraud.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) is constitutional, as it secures equal representation by distributing authority equally among board members and does not unconstitutionally constrain the judiciary, providing sufficient safeguards against fraud.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Election Law § 9-209 (2) (g) is constitutional and does not violate the equal representation mandate or principles of judicial review.

title: Fossella v. Adams
description: Whether Local Law 11, which allows non-citizens to vote in New York City municipal elections, is constitutional under the New York State Constitution, specifically Article II, Section 1, which plaintiffs argue limits voting to citizens, and defendants argue is a floor that can be expanded by local home rule.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that Local Law 11 violates Article II, section 1 of the New York State Constitution by limiting voting to citizens, that it cannot supersede the New York State Election Law, and that it violates the Municipal Home Rule Law by changing the method of voting without a public referendum.
defendant_argument: The defendants (City Council and Intervenors) argued that Article II, section 1 of the New York State Constitution merely provides a floor for voting rights, not a ceiling, and that Article IX (home rule powers) allows localities to expand the franchise to non-citizens for local elections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that Local Law 11 is unconstitutional because the New York State Constitution restricts voting to citizens.

title: Stefanik v. Hochul
description: Whether New York's Early Mail Voter Act, which permits all registered voters to vote early by mail, violates the New York Constitution by allowing voting methods beyond those historically understood or explicitly permitted.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the Early Mail Voter Act is unconstitutional because the New York Constitution historically mandated in-person voting and limits absentee voting to specific circumstances, and a recent ballot initiative to allow universal mail-in voting was rejected by voters.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Act is constitutional, as the Constitution does not explicitly prohibit mail-in voting, especially after the 1966 amendment removed the in-person voting requirement, and the legislature has broad powers to regulate elections.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that New York's Early Mail Voter Act is constitutional and does not violate the State Constitution.

title: People v. Watkins
description: Whether trial counsel was constitutionally ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification instruction at the close of the trial.
plaintiff_argument: The People (respondent) argued that trial counsel was not ineffective because, at the time of Watkins' trial, such an instruction was discretionary, not mandatory, and thus counsel's failure to request it did not constitute an egregious single error of ineffective assistance.
defendant_argument: Mark Watkins (appellant) argued that his trial counsel was constitutionally ineffective for failing to request a cross-racial identification instruction, especially given the cross-racial nature of the identification and the widely understood importance of such charges.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, upholding Mark Watkins' conviction.

title: People v. Debellis
description: Whether Anthony Debellis received ineffective assistance of counsel because his attorney failed to request a jury instruction on the statutory defense of voluntary surrender for criminal possession of a weapon, instead pursuing a meritless common-law defense.
plaintiff_argument: Counsel was not ineffective because the defendant was not entitled to a voluntary surrender instruction, and counsel's overall performance was not deficient.
defendant_argument: Counsel was ineffective for failing to request the voluntary surrender defense instruction, which was supported by trial testimony, and instead pursuing an inapplicable temporary and lawful possession defense, thereby depriving him of a fair trial.
decision_outcome: The order of the Appellate Division is reversed, and a new trial is ordered for Anthony Debellis.

title: People v. Rodriguez
description: Whether police interference with a bicyclist constitutes a seizure under federal and state constitutions, requiring reasonable suspicion of a criminal offense or probable cause of a Vehicle and Traffic Law violation.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff (defendant in the original case) argued that the police stop was an unlawful seizure because the officers lacked reasonable suspicion of criminal activity or probable cause of a traffic violation, and therefore the recovered gun and his statements should be suppressed.
defendant_argument: The defendant (The People) argued that the police encounter was a justified common-law inquiry, not a seizure, or that the officers had sufficient 'founded suspicion' for the stop.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, granted the defendant's motion to suppress the gun and statements, and dismissed the indictment, ruling that a police stop of a bicyclist is a seizure requiring reasonable suspicion or probable cause.

title: Hoffmann v. New York State Independent Redistricting Commission
description: Whether the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) has a continuing constitutional duty to prepare and submit new legislative redistricting plans for future elections, or if the court-drawn maps from the 2022 election are the exclusive and decade-long remedy.
plaintiff_argument: The IRC has a continuing constitutional duty to prepare and submit a second redistricting plan, even though the 2022 congressional map was judicially adopted, because the court-drawn maps were only an interim remedy for the 2022 election.
defendant_argument: The IRC's deadline to submit a second redistricting plan passed on February 28, 2022, making any current attempt to compel them unconstitutional and untimely, and the court-ordered redistricting plan from Harkenrider is the exclusive remedy that should remain in effect until the 2030 census.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, compelling the Independent Redistricting Commission to reconvene and submit a second redistricting plan and implementing legislation by February 28, 2024.

title: Police Benevolent Association v. City of New York
description: Whether section 10-181 of the Administrative Code of the City of New York, which criminalizes the use of certain restraints by police officers during an arrest, violates the New York Constitution on either preemption or due process grounds.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the local law is unconstitutional because it is preempted by state laws governing police arrest authority and is void for vagueness, particularly regarding the compression of an arrestee's diaphragm, failing to provide adequate notice of prohibited conduct.
defendant_argument: The City argued that the local law is a proper exercise of its home rule authority, is not preempted by state law, and is not vague because police officers receive training on the prohibited conduct.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Administrative Code § 10-181 is constitutional and is neither preempted by state law nor void for vagueness.

title: Stevens v. New York State Division of Criminal Justice Services
description: Whether the legislature's grant of rulemaking authority to the Commission on Forensic Sciences was sufficient to authorize the Commission's promulgation of the Familial DNA Search Regulations.
plaintiff_argument: The Commission lacked the statutory authority to promulgate Familial DNA Search Regulations, which are arbitrary and capricious, and infringe on privacy, particularly for African-Americans, thus violating the separation of powers doctrine.
defendant_argument: The Commission had the statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations, which were a proper exercise of its delegated power and not arbitrary or capricious.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order and dismissed the petition, ruling that the Commission had the statutory authority to promulgate the Familial DNA Search Regulations.

title: People v. Regan
description: Whether the People's four-year pre-indictment delay in a rape case violated the defendant's constitutional right to prompt prosecution.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that the delay was not a due process violation, or was justifiable for investigation, and that the defendant did not demonstrate special prejudice.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the excessive and largely unexplained pre-indictment delay violated his constitutional right to prompt prosecution, regardless of a showing of special prejudice.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order and dismissed the indictment, finding that the People's unexplained delay violated the defendant's right to prompt prosecution.

title: Owner Operator Independent Drivers Association v. NYS Department of Transportation
description: Whether New York regulations requiring electronic logging devices (ELDs) in commercial motor vehicles and authorizing warrantless inspections of ELD data violate the State Constitution's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argues that New York's ELD rule, which mandates warrantless inspections of ELD data, constitutes an unreasonable search and seizure under the State Constitution and fails to adequately limit the frequency of such searches.
defendant_argument: The defendant argues that the ELD rule's warrantless inspections fall under the administrative search exception to the warrant requirement for pervasively regulated industries and are constitutional under the State Constitution.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that the New York regulations adopting the ELD rule, which authorizes warrantless inspections, are facially constitutional and do not violate the State Constitution's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.

title: St. Lawrence Cnty. v. City of Ogdensburg
description: Whether Local Law No. 2-2021 of City of Ogdensburg, which repealed a prior local law opting out of the application of Real Property Tax Law (RPTL) article 11, is inconsistent with RPTL 1150 or otherwise unconstitutional under the home rule article of the New York State Constitution.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, St. Lawrence County, argued that Local Law No. 2 was inconsistent with RPTL 1150 and impaired the County's powers by unlawfully shifting the burden of enforcing and collecting delinquent City and School District taxes without an agreement, violating the New York Constitution and Municipal Home Rule Law.
defendant_argument: The defendant, City of Ogdensburg, argued that Local Law No. 2 is valid and enforceable because RPTL article 11 allows a city to opt back in by repealing its prior opt-out law, and RPTL 1102 (6)(b) supports a county enforcing delinquent taxes for a city via its charter without requiring a special procedure or agreement under RPTL 1150.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Local Law No. 2 is not inconsistent with RPTL 1150 or unconstitutional, and that it properly effectuates a power granted to cities to revoke their initial opt-out from RPTL article 11.

title: People v. Johnson
description: Whether the police had reasonable suspicion to justify a level three stop and frisk of Tyquan Johnson under the De Bour framework, with the plaintiff arguing that the police action was justified and the defendant arguing it was not.
plaintiff_argument: The police action, including the stop and frisk, was justified at its inception and at every subsequent stage of the encounter leading to Mr. Johnson's arrest, based on his movements and appearance.
defendant_argument: The police lacked the requisite level of suspicion to justify an intrusion under any level of the De Bour framework, specifically that his actions did not constitute reasonable suspicion for a level three stop and frisk.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the police lacked reasonable suspicion for the stop and frisk, and dismissed the indictment against Tyquan Johnson.

title: Delgado v. State
description: Whether the Legislature unconstitutionally delegated its legislative authority to the Committee on Legislative and Executive Compensation by allowing the Committee's recommendations for state official salaries to become law without further legislative action, with plaintiffs arguing it is an unconstitutional delegation and defendants arguing it is a valid assignment of power.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that the enabling act unconstitutionally delegated legislative authority to the Committee and violated the constitutional requirement that legislative salaries be "fixed by law."
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the enabling act was a valid assignment of power to the Committee and did not exceed its authority, thus being constitutional.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the enabling act was not unconstitutional and that the Committee did not exceed its authority.

title: Harkenrider v. Hochul
description: Whether the legislature's congressional and state senate maps should be invalidated due to a failure to follow constitutional redistricting procedures and unconstitutional partisan gerrymandering.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that the 2022 maps were enacted through a constitutionally defective process because the Independent Redistricting Commission (IRC) failed to submit a second plan, and the legislature lacked authority to create its own. They also asserted that the congressional map was unconstitutionally gerrymandered to favor the majority party by packing and cracking voters.
defendant_argument: The State respondents argued that the petitioners lacked standing, that the IRC's failure did not remove the legislature's authority to enact redistricting plans, and that the petitioners could not prove the maps were unconstitutionally partisan.
decision_outcome: The court declared the congressional and state senate maps void, finding them to be procedurally unconstitutional and the congressional map also substantively unconstitutional due to partisan gerrymandering. The court ordered judicial oversight to facilitate the creation of new, constitutionally conforming maps for the 2022 election.

title: People v. Dawson
description: Whether Malik Dawson unequivocally invoked his indelible right to counsel during police interrogation, thereby invalidating his subsequent waiver of Miranda rights.
plaintiff_argument: Malik Dawson's inquiries and demeanor suggested only a conditional interest in speaking with an attorney, not an unequivocal invocation of his right to counsel, allowing his subsequent waiver of Miranda rights to be valid.
defendant_argument: Malik Dawson unequivocally and repeatedly asked to contact his lawyer, making any subsequent waiver of Miranda rights without counsel present invalid.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, upholding Malik Dawson's conviction and the lower courts' determination that he did not unequivocally invoke his right to counsel.

title: White v. Cuomo
description: Whether Interactive Fantasy Sports (IFS) contests constitute unlawful "gambling" under Article I, § 9 of the New York Constitution, which prohibits unauthorized gambling.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiffs argued that IFS contests involve a material degree of chance and are essentially bets or wagers on future contingent events outside participants' control, thus constituting prohibited gambling under the State Constitution.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that IFS contests are skill-based competitions where participants exercise substantial influence over the outcome through knowledge and strategy, and therefore do not fall under the constitutional prohibition against gambling.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that Article 14 of the Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law, which authorizes IFS contests, does not violate the New York Constitution's prohibition on gambling.

title: People v. Torres
description: Whether the New York City Right of Way Law, which imposes criminal liability based on ordinary negligence for drivers who injure pedestrians or bicyclists, violates due process or is preempted by state law.
plaintiff_argument: The People of the State of New York argued that the Right of Way Law is constitutional, that ordinary negligence is a sufficient mens rea for criminal liability, and that the law is not preempted by state law, falling within the City's delegated authority to regulate traffic.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that the Right of Way Law is unconstitutional because its ordinary negligence mens rea violates due process and that it is preempted by state law, specifically the Penal Law regarding culpable mental states and the Vehicle and Traffic Law regarding traffic infractions.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Term's decision, rejecting the defendants' constitutional challenges and upholding the validity of the Right of Way Law.

title: People v. Schneider
description: Whether a Kings County Supreme Court Justice had jurisdiction to issue eavesdropping warrants for defendant's cell phones, which were not physically present in New York, for the purpose of gathering evidence in an investigation of enterprise corruption and gambling offenses committed in Kings County.
plaintiff_argument: The People argued that eavesdropping warrants are executed in the geographical jurisdiction where law enforcement officers intentionally intercept communications, regardless of the physical location of the target or device.
defendant_argument: Schneider argued that the Kings County Supreme Court Justice lacked jurisdiction because his cell phones and call participants were not physically present in New York, meaning the warrants were not 'executed' in Kings County.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's order, ruling that the Kings County Supreme Court Justice had jurisdiction to issue the eavesdropping warrants.

title: Protect the Adirondacks! Inc. v. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation
description: Whether the state's plan for constructing approximately 27 miles of Class II community connector trails for snowmobile use in the Forest Preserve is permissible under the New York Constitution, with the plaintiff arguing it violates the 'forever wild' provision due to extensive tree cutting and land alteration, and the defendant arguing it is permissible as it balances protection and public access without substantially impairing the wild forest nature.
plaintiff_argument: The construction of the Class II trails, requiring the cutting and removal of thousands of trees, grading, and leveling, violates the 'forever wild' provision of the New York State Constitution.
defendant_argument: The planned trails are permissible as they balance protecting the Forest Preserve with allowing year-round public access, do not constitute a substantial destruction of timber, and do not impair the wild forest nature of the Preserve.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the Appellate Division's decision, ruling that the planned construction of 27 miles of Class II community connector trails for snowmobile use in the Forest Preserve is unconstitutional and cannot be accomplished without a constitutional amendment.

title: People v. Gordon
description: Whether a search warrant authorizing the search of "entire premises" implicitly permits the search of vehicles located on those premises, even if the vehicles are not specifically mentioned in the warrant.
plaintiff_argument: The People argue that a warrant for "entire premises" should implicitly authorize the search of vehicles found on the property, treating them like other containers, based on federal caselaw.
defendant_argument: Mr. Gordon argues that New York law requires search warrants to particularly describe the areas to be searched, and since the vehicles were not mentioned in the warrant or supporting affidavit, the search was unlawful.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the lower courts' decisions to suppress the evidence seized from the two vehicles, ruling that the search warrant did not authorize the search of the vehicles.
